1.title: Securing AI Services in Applications
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Securing A I Services in Applications. It covers the exam area Domain two: Security. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Request and manage access to A I services (two point three.one). Use data privacy controls to transmit data to A I services (two point three.two). Filter and control A I model inputs and outputs (two point three.three). Secure A I agent interactions (two point three.four). Protect sensitive content in monitoring logs during A I interactions (two point three.five). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Domain two: Security (twenty-six percent). Exam format: fifty scored questions, multiple choice and multiple response; a score of seven hundred twenty on a scale of one hundred to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official A W S Developer Associate (D V A-C three) exam guide.

1.title: Request and manage access
1.text: Request and manage access. Model access. Access to a foundation model must be requested or enabled for the account. I A M permissions. Grant bedrock Invoke Model (and related actions) only to the roles that need it, scoped to specific models. Least privilege. Separate roles for development, testing and production. Service control. Organization policies can allow or deny models or Regions.

1.title: Data privacy in transit and use
1.text: Data privacy in transit and use. The figure shows this: Private connectivity to an A I service through a V P C endpoint, with guardrails on input and output.

1.title: Data privacy in transit and use, continued
1.text: Data privacy in transit and use. V P C endpoint (A W S Private Link). Application traffic to the A I service stays on the A W S network, not the public internet. Encryption in transit. T L S for every call. No training on your data. Inputs and outputs sent to Bedrock are not used to train the base models; confirm and document this. Minimize data. Send only what is needed; redact P I I before sending. Exam tip: "Keep traffic to the A I service off the public internet" equals an interface V P C endpoint (Private Link).

1.title: Filtering inputs and outputs: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
1.text: Filtering inputs and outputs: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Guardrails apply policies to prompts and responses. Content filters. Block harmful categories in input and output. Prompt attack filter. Detect jailbreaks and prompt injection in the input. Denied topics. Block subjects you define, matched by meaning. Word filters. Block exact words and phrases (and a profanity list). Sensitive information filters. Detect P I I (and custom patterns) and block or mask it. Contextual grounding. Check that a response is grounded in the source.

1.title: Filtering inputs and outputs: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, continued
1.text: Filtering inputs and outputs: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. The Apply Guardrail A P I applies a guardrail to any text, without calling a model, so you can protect other models or your own content. Exam tip: Prompt injection is an attack in the input; the defense is the guardrail's prompt attack filter plus treating model output as untrusted. Mask P I I equals sensitive information filter.

1.title: Securing AI agent interactions
1.text: Securing A I agent interactions. An A I agent can call tools (A P Is, databases). The risks grow because the agent acts. Tool-use authorization. Give the agent only the tools and permissions it needs; authorize each tool call (for example, with identity and a gateway). Session isolation. Separate each user's session so data and context never mix (Agent Core Runtime runs sessions in isolated environments). Human-in-the-loop. Require a person's approval before sensitive actions (payments, deletions, access changes).

1.title: Protect sensitive content in logs
1.text: Protect sensitive content in logs. Monitoring is useful but logs can leak prompts and responses. Decide what to log. Model invocation logging is optional; log only what you need. Mask or redact P I I. Use Cloud Watch Logs data protection or guardrail masking. Encrypt logs with K M S and restrict access. Logs are data too. Set retention. Do not keep sensitive logs forever. Exam tip: A V P C endpoint keeps traffic private; a guardrail filters content; an approval step protects sensitive agent actions. Match the control to the risk.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An application must call Amazon Bedrock without sending traffic over the public internet. What should the developer configure? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: An interface V P C endpoint for Bedrock. A V P C endpoint (Private Link) keeps traffic on the A W S network.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A chatbot must never discuss a competitor's pricing. Which Guardrails policy fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Denied topics. Denied topics block subjects defined by meaning.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. User input could contain "ignore previous instructions". Which control addresses this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Prompt attack filter. The prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks and injections.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Model responses sometimes contain customers' phone numbers. Which policy masks them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Sensitive information filters. Sensitive information filters detect P I I and block or mask it.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An agent can issue refunds. What is the best safeguard for large refunds? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A human approval step before the action. Human-in-the-loop approval protects sensitive actions.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Logs of A I interactions contain personal data. What should the team do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Mask or redact it, encrypt the logs and restrict access. Protect sensitive content in logs with masking, encryption and access control.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which technology keeps A I traffic off the public internet? Answer: A V P C endpoint (A W S Private Link). Question two. Name two Guardrails policies. Answer: For example content filters and sensitive information filters (also denied topics, word filters, prompt attack filter, contextual grounding). Question three. What does Apply Guardrail do? Answer: Applies a guardrail to any text without invoking a model.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name two ways to secure an A I agent. Answer: Tool-use authorization, session isolation, human-in-the-loop approval. Question five. Is Bedrock model invocation logging on or off by default? Answer: Off by default (it is optional). Question six. Is A I governance design on the exam? Answer: No, it is out of scope.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Access: enable model access; least-privilege I A M per model. Privacy: V P C endpoint, T L S, minimize and redact data. Guardrails: content, prompt attack, denied topics, words, sensitive info, grounding; Apply Guardrail. Agents: tool authorization, session isolation, human approval. Logs: log only what you need, mask, encrypt, restrict, set retention.
